utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-8-PT, the Prosecutor versus Damir Dosen and Dragan Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the transcript reflect that the case is late in starting ten minutes because counsel was not properly robed and robes had to be provided. That was Mr. Vucicevic. Mr. Vucicevic, you've been here long enough to know that you have to have robes before you appear in this Court. Would you kindly equip yourself with them. You have been doing cases here, to my knowledge, over two years and you should have robes. Yes, we'll hear the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Brenda Hollis, Kapila Waidyaratne, and Daniel Saxon appear on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Dusan Vucicevic, appearing for the accused Dragan Kolundzija from Chicago, Illinois, United States. Your Honour, if I just make -- address the point that you just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for not having had a robe. I will buy one. And I had rented a robe when I was on a previous trial so therefore, you know, I didn't have one available. I was borrowing one so far, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am Vladimir Petrovic, lawyer from Belgrade, appearing here for Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a hearing for a series of motions. First of all, a motion, motions rather, in relation to the amended attachment to the indictment. Secondly, a Prosecution motion for admission of documentary evidence. Thirdly, a Prosecution motion for judicial notice. Fourthly, a motion for severance of the indictment on behalf of Mr. Kolundzija. Today is set aside for oral argument in relation to the motions. These arguments can be short because there have been extensive written submissions in relation to all the motions which we have to deal with and the Court has read them. So anything said today should be supplementary to what is in the written submissions, and there is not to be any repetition. Now, it may be convenient to deal with the matters in this way, first of all, to deal with the two motions concerned with the indictment, that is, the motions in relation to the attachments, and then to deal with Mr. Kolundzija's motion for severance. Starting, then, with the motions in relation to the attachment, we have before us submissions on behalf of both accused. We have the Prosecution's response, and a Defence reply to that response. Now, as I said, those documents set the arguments out very fully, and I shall call on the Defence first to see if there is anything they want to add to supplement to the argument and submissions. Mr. Petrovic, I think you come first on the indictment now. Is there anything you'd like to add to what has already been argued?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I endeavoured to explain clearly the position of Damir Dosen's Defence in our submissions and to indicate what I believe are omissions of the Prosecution. However, while risking to repeat myself, I believe it is very important what the Chamber needs to bear in mind is Count 4 to 7 of the indictment; that is, in what does an attachment relate to Counts 4 to 7 of the indictment? These are events as of the 25th of June or around the 25th of June whereas in the counts we have the events which cover the whole period of the Keraterm camp. It contradicts the text of the indictment so will you please bear that in mind when you rule on our motions regarding the contents and formatting to the amendment of the indictment. I have already put everything else I have to say in written form, so I do not want to speak any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic, for dealing with the matter so succinctly. So that we have your arguments in mind, what you are really saying is this, as I understand it, is that the amended version of the attachment, in effect, amounts to an amendment of the indictment and, accordingly, the Prosecution should follow the amendment procedure. Is that right, that's the central submission which you make?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, I have to read the transcript because I think the interpretation it was not adequately said what you just told us. Two things are basic in my submission, the first thing is the manner in which the attachment was incorporated in the indictment so this is something that can be done only by the Prosecutor on the basis of the decision of the Chamber, this is the first thing. And the second is that the attachment is much longer than Counts 4 to 7 of the indictment. They cover events which go far beyond Counts 4 to 7 of the amended indictment. I believe it's paragraph 25 of the amended indictment. That is, it covers events from the beginning of June to the end of July and even early August whereas paragraph 25 of the indictment says clearly that the event concerned happened on or around the 25th of June, 1992. So I think this is a major shortcoming and there are quite a number of other inconsistencies which are listed in my written submission and I should like to ask the Chamber to bear in mind these things when considering the reply to our motions. I am not sure whether I understood your previous question, so if you want, will you please be so kind as to repeat it, and then I'll try to be even more clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you are saying, as I understand it, is that the Prosecution should be applying to amend the indictment, and therefore should follow the amendment procedure, and that would allow you, in due course, to put forward various motions about the amendment. I know that you also say that there's a failure to clarify, and you also say there are new factual allegations and also a new type of responsibility is introduced. But in effect, the centre of your submission is that this amounts to amendment and therefore that procedure should be followed. And that's what you're asking us to do, to say the indictment should be amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. You're quite right. The procedure of indictment amendment, as prescribed by the Rules, was not complied with. In your decision of the 10th of February, you ordered the Prosecution to incorporate the attachment -- to incorporate the attachment into the indictment, that the only way to do that was to incorporate the amendment into the indictment, and it was not done in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honour, Judge May, I adopt your nutshell summary of Mr. Petrovic's argument as the essence of Kolundzija's Defence opposing the amended attachment. However, there is a factual setting that came up in the Prosecutor's response which needs emphasising, because the Prosecutor is casually considering that the attached amendment charges additional 25 murders on the morning on 25th of July. That fact is not contained in the amended amendment -- in the amended indictment. That factual setting was contained in the original indictment. That factual setting has been dealt with in some of the pleadings prior to the amendment; therefore, the very fact that there is 25 victims that are nameless, and in order to accord them due respect and dignity, we would demand that the new amendment should be set. At the same time, to accord justice to my client, who has not been responsible for anything, in particular for this act, because by Prosecution's very own witness statements that have been disclosed to us early on in the material which was appended to the confirmed indictment, the Prosecutor's witness says that did not happen on my client's shift. A second point, Your Honour, is a theory of the case of common conduct. And theory of the case of common conduct has not been at all dealt in a manner that you have requested in your order, to delineate the nature of the conduct and specify the responsibilities. So these two men are charged for all that happened in Keraterm. Just using sheer logic, if that is correct, one of them should be discharged today, because they were not on duty at all times together. How could we defend against such an indictment? How could we prepare? Your Honours, and most importantly, the amended attachment, if you take it and look at it, please, contains, in the last column, named criminal responsibility, delineation of responsibility. And all of them refer to the Article 7(1) and (3), and none of them refer to the Article 5. So if the Prosecutor had followed your orders, by implication it seems that indictment pursuant to the Article 5 has been abandoned. Counts have been abandoned. Or when we connected with our later motions for separation of counts, this is exactly what we are talking. We are talking of separation of counts, and count -- and any responsibility pursuant to count 5 is non-existent here. But I will have more about that later. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A few very brief points. Regarding the point made by counsel for accused Dosen, to the extent the counsel argues about other inconsistencies in the schedule, we rely on our brief and we disagree with their position. However, in regard to the point that counsel makes about counts 4 to 7, we agree with counsel that the schedule goes beyond the scope of paragraph 25, counts 4 to 7, and we agree that in so doing it went beyond the scope of what Your Honours ordered us to do. We do not seek to amend, to enlarge the scope of counts 4 to 7, and we will clarify the particulars in regard to paragraph 25 only. So on that point only, we do agree with counsel for accused Dosen. In regard to arguments made by counsel for accused Kolundzija, we suggest in part those arguments were arguments on the facts of the case, and this is not the proper forum for that. In relation to the comments regarding the schedule and the 25 July murders, unless there are questions, the Prosecution believes it has adequately dealt with that in the submission made in writing to the Chamber. In regard to the attacks on the doctrine of common purpose, the Prosecution also relies on its written submissions regarding those attacks. We will point out to Your Honours, we believe the comments made today continue to manifest a misunderstanding and a misapprehension, and confuse the crimes alleged under Articles 3 and 5 with modes of liability that are set forth in Articles 7(1) and 7(3). Your Honour's order dealt with modes of liability under Article 7(1) and 7(3). Therefore, it would have been inappropriate for us to put Article 5 or Article 3 in the added column. So we believe again the argument made by counsel for accused Mr. Kolundzija misapprehends the order and misapprehends the subject matter of Article 7 compared to the subject matter of Articles 3 and 5. Unless there are questions, Your Honour, we have no further submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: JUDGE BENNOUNA [Interpretation] Mr. Vucicevic, I'd like to ask you the following: Do you accept what the Prosecutor has just said, which is a mere reading of a professional lawyer of the Statute of this Tribunal? In other words, on the one hand, you have the definition or characterisation of crimes, as is the case in statutes in many jurisdictions, criminal jurisdictions; and on the other hand, there's the type of individual liability, 7(1) and 7(3), which apply to any of the crimes concerned and characterised. Mr. Vucicevic, did you not confuse the two types of concepts: on the one hand, the characterisation of crimes, and, on the other, the individual criminal liability, which are two different matters? Indeed, we do have in our Statute Article 5 which you mentioned, Article 3 as well, Article 2, which define crimes under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, and then we have the type of individual criminal responsibility or liability, which are two different things. This was my first question. Second question. It deals with the common purpose doctrine. This matter does not really concern the indictment. It does not have anything to do with it inasmuch as it here revolves -- or deals with arguments to be adduced in relation to the crimes concerned and it relates to the type of characterisation that could be given when it comes to arguments. Therefore, it has nothing to do either with the indictment or with the list of the crimes as they are. It is a matter to be determined later. Some kind of a principle of criminal law which makes it possible to characterise a criminal conduct. So this does not have any bearing on this matter now or does not have any direct bearing on the indictment as such. So these were the two questions I wanted to put to you, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in taking your question -- first question first, I'm fully cognizant on the -- of the individual culpability under the Article 7(1) and (3), (1) being the direct and personal acts of the accused and 7, as you indicated in your order of February 10th, acts that derive, therefore derivative from his command -- however, in Article 5, there are two elements of crime; one is widespread persecution allegedly planned and instigated by the unit of a government; and second, acts of individual. Then again, it could be an individual very personal and the command authority to apply those crimes. So that's my argument, even though the Article 7 deals with the acts that are individual responsibility, the element of Article 5 also contained that element because the second element is widespread planned by the unit of a government committed against civil population during an act of war. So to me, if that is a common understanding, and I would accept it. However, even though as enumerated the acts, the personal acts under Article 7(1) and 7(3) are insufficient because they are vague and do not address the points that you requested in your order of February 10. That's my response to your question. And it's impossible to prepare a defence against it. Because in particular, my client, Mr. Kolundzija it charges him for everything that happened from the beginning to very end for -- from May 30th through September or what actually -- you know, the Keraterm disband around August 6th, so it charges him for everything. He was -- if he was a commander of the camp, then perhaps it would have been applicable, but only a part of the time he was appointed as shift commander, and as such, this is vague and impossible to prepare a Defence. What basically that elements we -- I understand the facts are for the trial, but the facts have been disclosed to us and these words have been given to us. The facts are the essence of everything that takes place here and without looking at them, we could allow the Prosecutor only on extremely weak facts against my case to proceed or the trial that is going to be perhaps six months long and that's why looking -- having an eye on the facts and interpreting procedure, we will arrive to the substance in justice. The answer to your second question, Your Honour, I -- if you would kind of clarify it because, with all due respect, I did not fully understand it. If you would just clarify your question a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was a very simple question. The indictment has to specify as a rule what the type of crime is, what the individual criminal liability is of a given person who might have committed such a crime. The doctrine of common purpose, in other words, the fact that an individual has participated in the commission of an act together with other individuals with a common purpose of criminal type; that is, a doctrine which is not connected, not directly connected with the indictment. It is a characterisation of a contact which can be argued by either party at trial. It has no direct bearing and does not derive directly from the indictment. That was the nature of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with you in part, and disagree in part. I agree with you in part that the doctrine that could be argued by both parties and that derives -- the implication of the doctrine derives from the presentation and finding of fact by the -- you respected, Honourable Judges. However, when it comes to this case in particular, the doctrine of common purpose sways across and puts the balance of the case within the purview of Article 5 that all what had happened there was a common purpose and therefore responsibility while the doctrine of common purpose is recognised by this Tribunal and by the appellate decision in Tadic distinguishes three different varieties, modalities of the common purpose. And looking at the indictment and what does it charge under Article 5 and Article 7. And having doctrine of common purpose some place in between, I believe the doctrine of a common purpose must be or at least factual situation underpinning the doctrine of common purpose must be delineated in the indictment. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, there is just one matter, so that I have your concession right, this is in relation to Mr. Dosen, paragraph 25 of the amended indictment, and what you're saying is that you are prepared to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. In the schedule, we went beyond that one incident and we are prepared to clarify that and conform to the order which would have limited us to that one instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Thank you very much. We'll consider this matter and give our ruling in due course. The next motion is Mr. Vucicevic's in relation to severance, and we have your motion, Mr. Vucicevic, of the 22nd of May and we have the Prosecution response of the 5th of June. Now, is there anything you would like to add today?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to clarify the -- our submissions because indeed there is a ground for severance of counts because the severance of counts would be the severance of counts based on the Article 5 and based on the 7. The Prosecutor had used what had happened in Prijedor or what the citizens of Prijedor of ethnic Serbian ethnicity have done to citizens of nonethnic to bootstrap, basically, nonexistent evidence of what my client had done to his inmates at Keraterm. And considering the basic fairness, if there is no evidence as to one count or there is very limited evidence as to one count which is of -- which would preclude a long and drawn out trial on another count, because indeed, in count number 5, the Prosecutor must prove both elements, personal acts to further and promote persecution of the ethnicity. But this has to be done by personal acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that we have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. So that we have your submissions, you're saying that the trial should take place on the events in the camp first, dealing with the personal, alleged personal responsibility of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is very practical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There should be a trial on that and that the Trial Chamber should make a ruling, do I understand this right? If there were no evidence, that would bring the trial to an end without the necessity of calling any evidence on the more widespread aspects of the allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would be, you know, our proposal to you. Because, you know, looking -- because now we have a full disclosure, almost a full disclosure, and what I have found there and we are prepared in chambers to give you offer of proof of defence evidence which is overwhelming. I am personally overwhelmed what had happened, and I would not want to kind of expose this Chamber to unnecessary waste of time because this is -- this is not going to turn on what witnesses are going to testify to what had happened in the city and what had happened, but it's going to turn what were the acts of the accused. If there are no culpability, then your -- this is not a jury trial where we are going to say well, jury here has to understand the background. You have reviewed the case. You have sat on judgements in other matters concerning this occurrence of fact so this would be rather expeditious. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, do you want to say anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. We have nothing particular to say with regard to this motion, and it will be your ruling regarding the motion of Mr. Kolundzija's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hollis, is there anything you want to add to your response?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, the Prosecution again submits that counsel is misapprehending the legal import of Articles that charge crimes and Article 7 that discussions characterisations of individual criminal responsibility, that is to say, modes of liability. In terms of this bifurcation that is recommended, we ask Your Honours what kind of rulings would you make? You can't find him guilty of anything or not guilty of anything assessed under Article 5 after we hear about the camps only because in order to find someone guilty of any of the substantive offences under Article 5, you also have to find that common elements exist, the same is true with Article 3. So we suggest that there would be no savings of anything to do what the accused suggests because the Chamber would be in no position to make any rulings. Secondly, even if, somehow, some limited rulings were to be made, then we bring all the same witnesses back to discuss the other elements of the crimes that were charged. So we suggest that again, this motion should be denied. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vucicevic, I have, of course, read your submissions and conclusions. It comes down to this: You say you have to disassociate individual criminal liability of your client, Mr. Kolundzija, from what you call the derivative liability. So I don't know how that can be translated into French, maybe indirect liability, "responsibilite indirect", but the first question I want to put to you is as follows: Are you not making a confusion between the context of the crime and responsibility? Because when there is widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population in Article 5, what we are, in fact, dealing with is the global setting, the global context which is such that a person, an individual, who has committed an individual act and therefore incurs individual liability when it is situated in a generalised or widespread attack on a civilian population is then guilty of a crime against humanity and not of ordinary crime. So my question is: There must be some kind of confusion because here we judge about the individual liability of Mr. Kolundzija. We are not judging about the global context. So here is my question: Are you not of the view that the issue of the generalised widespread and systematic attack on civilian population has not already been established in the case law of this Tribunal; for instance, in relation to the events in Prijedor. You mentioned the Tadic case where there has already been an appeal and a decision at that stage. Could there not be judicial notice taken of those facts? This may avoid us coming to the issue of the widespread and systematic attack on civilian population and if we can have such judicial notice, we could save going back to all the events that have taken place in Prijedor, and we could deal only with the individual direct criminal liability to know whether there is participation by Mr. Kolundzija or whether there is a link between Mr. Kolundzija and the events in question. So this is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I were to concede that the common elements of a crime, as adjudicated in Tadic's, was correct, veritable and just, I would be -- I would consider that I am exceeding to the political expediency which is not a matter for a judicial body to partake in. Neither would I consider myself worthy of a counsel being in front of you to suggest something like that. And why am I saying this? Because Defence counsel in Tadic's case, the matter that I have reviewed in print and in tape entirely, has never put one question in cross-examination on these matters. Moreover, I have investigated these matters in a previous case in detail. And there is, because Article 5 is asking that there is a systematic and widespread attack which presumed that there was a planning for such an attack. And I have found none of those elements. Perhaps there was -- there were allegedly crimes committed, but times when, how, and how many people were released from the camps and especially at the beginning would not comport to those findings, because if we were -- if I were to concede to something like this, I would deprive this Tribunal and I would deprive the world to hear the truth. However, going to the first part of your question, Your Honour, is whatever had happened in Prijedor concerning the common design for a systematic alleged persecution would -- it's not relevant when it comes to the trial of my client, because there are two elements to be proven there, that he furthered that persecution by his acts. If he did not further it, but had resisted and -- JUDGE BENNOUNA [Interpretation] Sorry. Excuse me for interrupting you, because we want to proceed most swiftly. My question was a very simple one. In order to prove that there was a link between your client, Mr. Kolundzija, and the systematic and widespread attack against a civilian population, we must first have proven that there was such an attack, that it has happened, and that there was such a widespread and systematic attack on the population, and only then can we move to see whether there is a link between such an attack and Mr. Kolundzija. So either we adduce such evidence in the one and the same trial or we go from the principle that there has been judicial notice as to -- to show that there was such a widespread and systematic attack. That would be the starting point, and only then would we see whether there was a link between your client and the attack. We can't go the other way around. That has just been said to you. You cannot appreciate the behaviour or the link between Mr. Kolundzija and something that has not been established yet. That's the logic about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have heard your opinion, but I respectfully disagree with it. And I respectfully disagree because there is a burden of proof on the part of the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor must prove every element of crime beyond a reasonable doubt. So whatever had happened in commonality in Prijedor, that has to be proven by reasonable doubt, just as his personal acts in furtherance must be proven. JUDGE BENNOUNA [Interpretation] Very well. [Technical difficulty] -- of a judicial notice of those facts. You are of the view that the Prosecutor must adduce all evidence on all elements, must prove that there was a systematic and widespread [as interpreted], must have to adduce evidence as to the individual criminal liability of Mr. Kolundzija. You say that the Prosecutor must adduce evidence of the crime, but is it possible to disassociate the two elements by judging them separately, by trying them separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, it's possible, because if Mr. Kolundzija was participating in gathering the population and bringing him to Keraterm, if he participated in political bodies, if he participated in the military as well and the police, if he volunteered for his duty, if any of those facts were alleged, you would have had connection between common elements and his personal activities. We only hear that he was a shift commander for a certain part in that. And by his acts, by the facts that were found in the Prosecutor's evidence, says that he had helped many and harmed none, barring the finding of fact what had happened on July 24th. That's what I am driving at. I'm driving at very efficient and fair. If this was a jury, Your Honour, I would agree with you, but a learned court like this could, you know, make a finding of fact on one set of issues and then move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. We'll give our ruling on this matter. The next two matters concern Prosecution motions, one for the admission of documentary evidence, one for judicial notice. Ms. Hollis, it may be convenient to deal with the admission of documentary evidence first.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should say, we've seen the various submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will be brief on that. And my colleague, Mr. Saxon, will deal with that issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning. In this case, although the accused are charged for their specific acts or omissions within the Keraterm camp, the events that occurred inside the Keraterm camp were inherently linked to the events that were occurring outside the camp in the broader Prijedor region during the relevant time period of this indictment. The documents offered for admission by the Prosecution are relevant and probative to demonstrate the existence of the common or, if you will, jurisdictional elements of the crimes charged: the existence of an armed conflict and the existence of a widespread or systematic policy to persecute non-Serbs in Prijedor in order to drive them out of that part of Bosnia during 1992. In addition, the Prosecution submits that these documents are relevant and probative to establish the nexus.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading, for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. In addition, these documents are relevant and probative to establish the nexus between the ongoing armed conflict, the policy of persecution, and the unlawful confinement and mistreatment of Muslims and Croats in the Keraterm camp. Your Honour, I think there's one document that perhaps captures very well the Prosecution's submissions as to relevant and probative value of the entire submission. That would be document 4.25, and I have made copies and brought them to the Trial Chamber today. If I can ask my colleague from the registrar to provide them to the Court and to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it also be provided to the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would be willing to give my copy to the interpreter's booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. They should have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Document 4.25 is a document from July 1992, an order given by the president of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor saying that all prisoners who are confined in the Omarska and Keraterm camps and who are expected of being involved were being involved in the armed rebellion should also be dismissed from their employment. Your Honour, this document, as do many other documents, in the Prosecution's submission, establishes that the Keraterm inmates were subjected to economic persecution based on their unlawful confinement in the Keraterm camp. And this unlawful confinement, as other documents demonstrate, was itself the product of the intent to discriminate against Muslims and Croats and to cleanse the Prijedor region of its non-Serb population. So as you read these documents, the relevance, the probative value, the indicia of reliability is present on its face. These documents begin to talk to each other and speak to each other. And based on the Tadic decision on the Defence motion on hearsay from the 5th of August, 1996, as well as a decision from our Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski case from February 1999, the Prosecution would submit that they're admissible at this stage of the proceeding outright. Should the Trial Chamber decide that these documents should not be admissible outright, alternatively, the Prosecution suggests that if the Defence can make, or chooses to make, specific supportable challenges to the authenticity of individual documents, the Defence could do so at trial, and the Prosecution could be permitted to respond to these challenges regarding authenticity during its rebuttal case. And thus at the end of the trial, the Trial Chamber could give each document the evidentiary weight that the Trial Chamber feels the evidence deserves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's my recollection that we've made that sort of order in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, you have, Your Honour. On the 17th of March, 1999, in case number IT-98-30, this same Trial Chamber made a similar -- virtually the identical resolution, based on the same documents, Your Honour, a motion for the admission of literally these same set of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you've heard a similar order, as mentioned just then by Mr. Saxon, was made in another case by this Trial Chamber. Is there any reason that we shouldn't make a similar order? The effect of it would be -- of course, as you know, hearsay is admissible in this Tribunal and has been admitted in innumerable cases. Documents are, on the whole, freely admitted. But clearly, if there is an issue, a genuine issue as to authenticity or reliability, or indeed relevance, then that is something which the opposing parties should be entitled to raise. So the proposed order would be to admit the documents but to order that you would be at liberty to challenge them on the grounds of relevance, authenticity, or reliability, during the trial. So as it were, the presumption is it would start with the documents being admitted, but on the other hand, you would have the chance, if there are grounds for doing so, of challenging them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you must have read the motion of Damir Dosen's defence relative to that matter, that is, the second part of that motion related to adjudicated facts, and that is where we address this matter. What you have said is also shown in that motion as a position of Defence. You have in mind the ruling taken in the case against Kvocka and others, and in a manner documents were admitted, but the Defence reserved the right to, when it comes to the Defence case -- Defence stage in the trial, to then challenge these documents, to challenge their authenticity, and present its evidence, which could then question the probative value of the document that we are referring to now. So the wording used in the Kvocka case with regard to identical material is quite agreeable to us, with, of course, this reservation. Just briefly, the document which was presented today, by the Prosecution today, is one of the rare documents, if not the only document, which establishes any kind of relationship between and link between Keraterm and Damir Dosen. That is, almost all the documents are documents about which the Dosen accused knows absolutely nothing or speak about events in which he did not participate in any way whatsoever, so that he simply cannot pronounce himself on them, because individuals and events described in them or mentioned in them are completely unknown to him. So that I should like to submit, as we did it already in our motion, to apply this procedure with regard to the documentary material proposed by the Prosecution. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any challenge, of course, is not limited to the calling of evidence. A challenge can be made, and probably should be made, if there is one, by way of cross-examination, if there is a relevant witness who can deal with the points raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I will start with your -- the latest comment, Judge May. Because if there is a relevant witness, then the document should be introduced to the relevant witness, because otherwise it puts a burden of proof on the Defence to search for the relevant witnesses that are more -- that are very likely to know the content of the Prosecutor's document. That's why, in the alternative to my submission, I have asked you that the Prosecutor first use the witnesses as -- that are familiar with these documents, to introduce them, or to use, if you decide to introduce -- to allow the Pre-Trial introduction, as you did in the Kvocka case, then the Prosecutor should be at liberty to present the witnesses to support who could be cross-examined about the content and the reliability of these documents. And on some documents the Defence might be bringing the witnesses. And upon the conclusion of the case, and before the closing arguments, I would respectfully ask you to expunge all those documents that have not been -- whose reliability and weight of their evidence have not been established by either direct presentation or cross-examination. Therefore, we would not have 225 documents which are indicating that there were political decisions, for which my client knows nothing about, to weigh heavily upon your decisions after the Prosecutor's argument, which I surmise the Prosecutor will be using all of those, you know, to present a closing argument. That's why I feel there would be basic prejudice. So a little bit of compromise, I think that would move us within the confines of the facts of this case. That is why this case is different from Omarska; therefore, your ruling should be so tailored. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE BENNOUNA [Interpretation] Mr. Vucicevic, in what you have just said, there is inevitably -- there are inevitably two types of documents in relation with the type of crimes concerned, the two types we have just mentioned: The widespread and systematic type of an attack and the link between such an attack and the accused. There are two types of documents. There are documents which may be of a general nature as to the context in order to lay the foundations of the context, the setting, and it is outside the camps. The general setting in which such criminal conduct was carried out. And then there are documents which have a direct bearing -- a direct relation to the accused, which may show his responsibility directly, and that has to be confirmed indeed by witnesses to be called during examination-in-chief or cross-examination. Do you not think that we should make such a distinction? We have documents of a general nature, establishing simply the setting or the context. Such documents do not need witnesses to be called for direct confirmation. But the authenticity of such documents, of course, if there is such indication, could always be challenged. So this was my question to you regarding these two types of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to answer this by using the Statute. I think Article 21 of the Statute guarantees the accused confrontation of the evidence to be presented against him. Whether that evidence is directed on the Article 7 and the Article 5 is still irrelevant because he has to have opportunity to cross-examine it, to challenge the weight of that evidence. Not the authenticity. We have more or less conceded authenticity for the purposes of pre-trial admission. However, for the weight of the evidence, because if we concede authenticity to be commingled with the relevance and proof of the weight of that evidence, if that evidence remains unchallenged on the docket, then we have violated Article 21. And I'm merely trying to assist this Trial Chamber to separate authenticity from our right to cross-examine the accuser. Even the document -- this accuser against my client. Even if that's background fact, how inaccurate. Somebody else did it, not him. But indeed, this is a grave accusation. Within the confines of sentencing, which we never think that we will get to, but -- based on our evidence. But even within the confines, because we have to think about this. So therefore we have to be given a chance to cross-examine this. And it is possible. There is five years that the war has seized, and motions have subsided, but there are still a few that think that wars should be won in the courtroom and not in the battlefield, but we can separate them and we can get the people to testify. Because it would please me to the utmost, in my professional career, to bring you the evidence upon which you can make a decision that's worthy of this Tribunal, a decision on this case and not on Tadic's case, because it was too close. I will get you the evidence from the attorneys in that case what kind of difficulties they had. That's why that was a hollow defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, why should these documents be admitted now and as against being admitted during the case when the evidence is being presented?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the purpose of expediting the trial, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that expedition is one matter. The general achievement of justice is also of paramount importance and this is the point which Mr. Vucicevic has been making.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct, Your Honour. If I might respond to one of the points that Mr. Vucicevic just made. Mr. Vucicevic sited Article 21. I believe he's referring to Article 21(E) regarding the right of accused in this Tribunal to cross-examine witnesses who testify against them. Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's submission that there's no need to call witnesses in order to have these documents admitted into evidence because the relevance, probative value and the reliability or if you will, authenticity is -- can be seen from the face of the documents, Your Honour. So we don't have, in this case, in the case of this material, we don't have a confrontation problem. That would be my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what is lost if the documents are not admitted now and they are sought to be adduced during the trial? I'm not clear as to what is the significant gain in expedition because, in any event, the Trial Chamber will have to assess the weight and reliability of the evidence in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The Court's July indulgence, please. Your Honour, I'm not sure if I understand your specific sense of timing but again, it is without trying to sound redundant, the Prosecution does not intend at this time to call witnesses to lay foundation for the admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suppose your argument would be that if you are forced to call witnesses to produce these 225 or whatever documents in the way which common lawyers are familiar with, a great deal of court time will be taken up, possibly unnecessarily on matters about which there are no dispute simply to produce documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is absolutely the Prosecution's position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And although it's right that, of course, it means that it is for the Defence to make a showing as to the documents as to why they should be challenged, and to that extent, it doesn't follow the common law rules. But then as we have often observed, we are not a common law jurisdiction. Very well, we'll consider this, having heard the submissions. The final submissions are in relation to judicial notice. Again, this is a Prosecution submission. Ms. Hollis, are you going to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly on our motion, we have set forth our rationale in that motion. We suggest that when you look at this motion, you look again at the obvious which is sometimes overlooked and that is Rule 94 allows an alternate means of proof, and that is proof of elements by accepting facts that have been determined in other proceedings. There is no requirement that these facts be determined at the appellate level although the majority of the facts that we have provided to you are facts that were set forward in the Tadic case and which were adopted at the appellate level on the Tadic appellate judgement. That, if you will, may give added weight to the argument we make, but it is not that an appellate court have ruled on the facts we are offering. Rule 94 indicates that these adjudicated facts may be entered to relate to matters at issue and that is what we are doing. We would also ask you to give particular attention to the following: The facts that we are asking you to review, in particular, the facts relating to the Tadic judgement adopted by the Appeals Chamber relate to the same opstina during the same period of time, with the same types of offences, with the same theory of the case, with the same groups involved. That is to say, Bosnian Serb offenders as part of Bosnian Serb ethnic cleansing, and with the same groups of victims, that is to say, Bosnian Muslims, and Bosnian Croats predominantly. In that case as well, it was noted that the camps were a part of the wider ethnic cleansing so that the facts we are asking you to judicially notice are directly on point in both cases. Contrary to assertions by Defence counsel, the Defence counsel in the a Tadic case did not accept blindly the facts that were found in the Tadic case. They did, through cross-examination and through putting on their own evidence, contest many of the issues that the Trial Chamber found, the facts that they found which were later adopted by the Appeals Chamber. We suggest that in at least one regard, the Tadic Appeal Chamber decision is binding precedent on this court. And that is to say that Tadic Appeals Chamber accepted the facts found at trial in specific in relation to their determination that there was an international armed conflict. We have not charged international armed conflict, but Articles 3 and 5 can apply in either international or internal. We suggest to you that the facts relating to armed conflict and the existence of an armed conflict have been found by the Tadic Trial Chamber in a case that is sufficiently similar, that it has binding effect on this Chamber unless or until one or both of the accused can come forward and show why the evidence in this case will be so different that this Trial Chamber should deviate from the binding precedent that has been established. We will also ask Your Honours to take particular note of the decision that was reached in the Kvocka case regarding judicial notice. We agree that there were dissimilarities in that circumstance because in the Kvocka case, the Defence counsel ultimately agreed to 444 of the facts put forward by the Prosecution. That is not the case in here. However, in making its decision, the Trial Chamber took note of the appeals counsel decision in the Tadic case, especially paragraph 148. Paragraph 148 of the Tadic appeals decision is the paragraph in which the Appeals Chamber accepts and relies upon the facts found by the Tadic Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber in Kvocka took a significant additional step which was not agreed to by the parties for the accused; that is, based on the judicially-noted facts, they proceeded to make findings of law as to those facts and decided upon elements of the offences. We suggest that that rationale would apply here. It is not necessary to take judicial notice only when opposing counsel agree to it. You may take judicial notice whether they agree or not. So we suggest it would be appropriate to take judicial notice unless, and unless Defence counsel can provide you with genuine ways that they intend to attack the evidence relied upon by the Tadic Appeals Chamber and the Celebici Trial Chamber or to show their own evidence to show that those facts are no longer trustworthy facts for this Tribunal to consider. Until such a thing is done, we suggest the better course of action would be to take judicial notice of the facts that we have put forward. Your Honours, if there are no questions, those are the comments the Prosecution would make on this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what you suggest, Ms. Hollis, is that we should, as it were, take provisional judicial notice. We should say that while it's open to the Defence to bring forward evidence or submissions in relation to matters, in the absence of such submissions, we would take judicial notice of the fact and of the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Conditional judicial notice I'm not sure about, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I mean either you take judicial notice or you don't. If you leave open the possibility, which seems to me sensible, that the Defence should have the ability to challenge some matter which you've judicially noticed, effectively you are not taking judicial notice, you're saying, well, we will take judicial notice unless. That's why I coined the expression provisional judicial notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I certainly understand the concept you are promoting. The Prosecution would suggest that in relation to that concept, which we believe is a valid appellate concept in that an appellate decision stands unless something comes up that would materially undermine it. We would suggest that perhaps with regard to the impact of the timing of the trial and the calling of witnesses, that perhaps the way it should be handled is that by way of what is anticipated in Article 65 ter, and that is that perhaps the timing of that portion of the Defence's, if you will, pre-trial brief would be brought forward so that before the beginning of the Prosecution's case, Your Honours would be and the Prosecution would be provided with the Defence's position as to how it would go about undermining these facts and these elements, by what means and what ways, which facts it would attack. So that before we put on our evidence, Your Honours would be able to determine if it appears likely that such an attack would be successful. And the reason the Prosecution suggests that is that all of the witnesses we call will have some evidence that is relevant to these broader elements, if you will, to these common or jurisdictional elements. If we wait until the close of our case to know whether we have to deal with them or not, we and this Trial Chamber could be faced with recalling all of these witnesses to put forward this evidence. If it appears likely that the challenge the Defence would make would have enough merit that you would go forward with it and would thus not take judicial notice, if we know that before we call our witnesses, we will elicit that evidence when they are here the first time and we won't have to recall them. So for that reason, perhaps if the 65 ter mechanism were used, Your Honours would be in a better position to make a more definitive ruling on judicial notice before the Prosecution commences its case. But certainly, Your Honour, we are in agreement with you when you say that, really, you'd have to look at what showing was made to make a final decision on it. When that showing should be made is the issue, I guess, that the Prosecution is raising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, here we have a case which I believe, should we follow the course of action proposed by the Prosecution, it would mean that before any evidence is brought before this Tribunal, that both the accused would be considered guilty. When considering adjudicated facts, we have several issues. There are points that need to be established completely in regard of Articles 3 and 5. There is a point which characterises the nature of the investigation centre in Keraterm which would complete and wrap up everything that concerns these two accused before any evidence is brought before this Trial Chamber, and that is contrary to all the rules of this Tribunal. We have tried to work with the Prosecution and we have tried to reach some agreements with the Prosecution. We can accept certain of the facts, but there are a number of them that are unacceptable for us. Most -- what is most unacceptable to us is the fact that most of these adjudicated facts are to be drawn from the Tadic case which are dated both historically and legally speaking when you review the entire case in its -- there was very little cross-examination regarding the facts that relate to the adjudicated facts was almost nonexistent. Also, the accused have to be guaranteed the right to present their own evidence and that the Trial Chamber weighs the relevance of the -- all the evidence presented. In the Kvocka case, there were some adjudicated facts but they were based on the agreement of the parties. There was no forcing of these adjudicated facts on the Defence. We need to review the -- all the facts based on the Articles 3 and 5 before any facts can be adjudicated. The order of the presentation of evidence has been -- the order of the presentation of evidence has been established, and I think that both sides need to present their side, and it will be the -- up to the Trial Chamber to then rule even though there are a number of adjudicated facts -- there are a number of points that are to be adjudicated from the Tadic case. We have a case that has not been finished, that has not been adjudicated per se, so we cannot proceed with the adjudicated facts based on that trial and that is another thing that I believe the Trial Chamber should take into consideration when ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I adopt in its entirety argument by my esteemed colleague Petrovic. In starting, I would just like to make a few remarks. The Prosecutor is arguing because most of these paragraphs have been found in the appellate decision in Tadic's case, that they are somehow -- they have a higher legal importance and value. Indeed, even though you have stressed this is not a common law court, but Appeals Chamber does not have a purview of fact finding; therefore, you, your learned Judges are sitting in judgement of the facts. Secondly, it has been the mark of the Prosecution that there was a cross-examination of the examination of the facts. I have just spoken two weeks ago when I met Mr. Kostic, who was assistant attorney in Tadic's case, who has assured me that he will give me an affidavit indicating that there was, indeed, a plan not to contest any of these by the lead counsel in that case. So if necessary, prior to your ruling, I shall submit you such an affidavit. And number three, the Prosecutor, it seems, you know, it's everything, you know, possible, and decent when the shoe is on the other foot. The counsel is -- for the Prosecution is offering and inviting us to give you an offer of proof on the element of Count 5 which I have suggested in my motion for severance to be given later. However, it was very silent when I offered to present you an offer of proof on the Count 7. And when I mentioned something here, when I mention decency. Before the jury, we argue a common sense. But some 45 years ago when it came to the matter of expediency, a very famous man, Prescott Bush, told a prosecutor United States Senate, "Do you have a decency, senator?" When we here, when everything else goes aside, have to adhere to that decency because that's what the justice is relying on. And argument was lacking it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, could you clarify one point for me, regarding paragraph 148? You mentioned it and you insisted on the paragraph in the appellate proceedings on the merits in the Tadic case. You said we had to refer to paragraph 148 because the latter of the Appeals Chamber takes judicial notice of facts as found by the Trial Chamber. You say that based on that, we could take up those facts and regard them as ours in our Trial Chamber in this case Kolundzija, Dosen. Are you not making a confusion between the relationship between a Trial Chamber and an Appeals Chamber in one and the same case, and the Trial Chamber in one case and a Trial Chamber in another? Indeed, I do not have paragraph 148 in front of me, but the Appeals Chamber is not supposed to try the facts as found by the Trial Chamber unless there is an error of fact upon which the attention of the Appeals Chamber is drawn. This is not the same for a Trial Chamber, because when you think of the relationship between a Trial Chamber and an Appeals Chamber, there you're dealing with one and the same case, the same people, the same facts, the same circumstances. Here in our case, we have at least one thing which is different, the people are not the same. Individuals are not the same. And it may be that the circumstances are not the same. This has to be established. Therefore, you invite us to make this transposition to take over some elements. Is it possible? Is it not against the logics? The analogy between two different things can lead to more confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we would suggest that what we're asking you to do is the essence of Rule 94, which says that a Trial Chamber may adopt facts and other proceedings where there weren't the same accused, where there weren't even the same charges. So what we're asking is that you do what Rule 94 allows you to do and we suggest it's appropriate to do in this setting. In regard to paragraph 148, the Prosecution initially said that in regard to the Tadic facts, the reality that the Appeals Chamber adopted and relied on those facts may give more weight to the Prosecution's argument, because we have not only had a Trial Chamber find the facts, but indeed the Appeals Chamber has reviewed those facts and has said they will rely on them. The other reason we specifically mention paragraph 148 of that decision is that in the Kvocka decision on judicial notice, the Trial Chamber takes particular note of the Appeals Chamber decision, and in particular of paragraph 148. Paragraph 148 indicates: "The Appeals Chamber does not see any ground for overturning the factual findings made in this case by the Trial Chamber and relies on the facts as stated in the judgement." Now, perhaps the wording "does not see any ground for overturning" comes back to the qualification that exists for any appellate decision. An appellate decision is binding unless a substantial ground can be shown as to why it would not be. And that's where we turn to the issue of 65 ter and the timing of the Defence's submission as to how they would go about overturning that decision or undermining its credibility. So we don't believe that we're confusing things here. We believe that the fact the Appeals Chamber did rely on those facts does give more weight to our argument, and that our argument is that this Trial Chamber should use Rule 94 to accept what other Chambers, either trial or Appeals, have found in this case, because they are relevant to the same circumstances. In regard to the second part of your question, Your Honour, that we have different people and perhaps the circumstances are different: If you will review carefully the facts that we are asking you to take judicial notice of, our purpose for those facts is to use those facts to prove the common elements or the jurisdictional elements; not what these particular accused did or did not do in the camps, but rather the jurisdictional or common elements. And indeed you can't find someone guilty here in this Tribunal unless you are satisfied that not only the underlying substantive elements of the individual crimes are proven, but that the common elements are proven. That's what makes these crimes crimes within our jurisdiction and not domestic crimes of murder or torture or rape. So that by finding the facts, we're asking you to judicially notice. You are not finding these accused guilty, because we have not proven the other elements that we need to prove. But we suggest to you that a Trial Chamber can judicially notice facts and then upon those facts make findings as to legal elements. But because of the type of elements we're asking you to consider and the type of facts, it would not be a finding of guilty, because the other elements of the underlying substantive offences have not yet been addressed or proven. And in regard to the point that was made that perhaps you're being asked to make a finding before any evidence is brought, the evidence on which we're relying are the facts we are asking you to judicially notice, and those facts are before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you are asking us to judicially notice them conditionally, until a showing is made.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What we are asking you is to judicially notice them. What we are accepting is that if the opposing party is able to make a showing that would undermine those facts, then it would be appropriate not to judicially notice them. And taking that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You would consider it; that's what you're really saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. Or if a showing is made in advance of the trial, then an initial decision could be made. Any decisions made pre-trial, of course, are always subject to reconsideration, and if evidence at trial turns out to dispute what has already been accepted. So we acknowledge that it may be necessary to do some type of provisional or conditional notice. We suggest that it need not be done until the Defence is able to show you the way in which they would undermine the facts that are to be noticed, and we think 65 ter is a good vehicle for that, 65 ter, part F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. We're not at school. If counsel has got a point, then they can make it, but I think we've finished the debate on judicial notice. We've heard both sides. Is there anything else that anybody wants to raise? I'm not encouraging you, because it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you believe that the previous topic is concluded, then no, but if it's still open to further submissions, then I have a couple of points to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. What the Prosecution is arguing of the common elements is precisely what the -- and the intent -- is precisely what the defence of Dosen is. If such common elements existed in Prijedor, he has nothing to do with it, and that is precisely the crux of our argument. But for us to be expected to present such evidence before the trial is contrary to the whole proceedings here, and we only ask to be given the right time and the opportunity to present such evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The invitation that the Prosecutor has given to you to admit this conditionally first would deprive us of-- would shift the burden of proof tremendously. We would not have the witness -- we could not cross-examine the witnesses that the Prosecutor otherwise would have brought in, and would put us in the position to prove and to disprove at the same time. This is not a decent invitation to you, Your Honour. If you have to live with the decision of making judicial notice on, as it is, decision is yours, but do not accept it conditionally. But I will submit you the affidavit indicating there was no defence. Vujin has talked to me throughout the appellate process and said that he had withheld facts throughout and part appeal contained new facts. This was -- that was the trial that had a lot of errors, but errors which came to -- into the judgement and on the facts that are so vital to my client. That's why I respectfully ask you not to take the notice. One more point, Your Honour, if you may. After the recess I would have some comments in the closed session, unrelated to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a hearing which is purely for hearing a motion, and I do not -- we don't propose to sit beyond this break. Now, if you've got any matters that you feel should be dealt with, they should be dealt with by the Pre-Trial Judge or a matter which you can put into writing. As far as the affidavit is concerned, we don't think that such an affidavit about the Tadic trial would assist us, and we will deal with the matter on those that are before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, we'll go into closed session now and we'll hear what it is you've got to say briefly.
